question: Who were the people Shuʿayb addressed in relation to Midian?

positions.position: They were a people distinct from Midian, and Shuʿayb was sent to both.
positions.reasons: Abū Zayd as reported by al-Thaʿlabī distinguishes Shuʿayb's own Midian from the nomadic Thicket people. Al-Wāḥidī's exegetes, al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Ālūsī, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī, and al-Sāmarrāʾī distinguish the groups; al-Wāḥidī cites 7:85 and 11:84, and al-Sāmarrāʾī adds 23:36. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah reports seven Thicket towns separate from Shuʿayb's Midian. Ibn Abī Ḥātim transmits al-Rabīʿ's account of a further mission to the Thicket herders. Ibn al-Jawzī reports Muqātil's sequence, Midian followed by the Thicket. Abū Ḥayyān reports a rural versus town distinction. Ibn Kathīr relays ʿIkrimah's two-mission story but calls it weak; he also relays a report attributed to the Prophet via ʿAbd Allāh b. ʿAmr calling them two nations, but calls it strange and doubts its prophetic attribution. Ibn al-Jawzī reports Muḥammad b. Kaʿb's canopy punishment for Midian, which would be a shared fate if the peoples differed. Al-Ālūsī calls Ibn ʿAbbās's equation of the two an unusual report.

positions.position: The Thicket people and Midian were the same community described by different names.
positions.reasons: Ibn Jarīr, reported by Ibn al-Jawzī, identifies them as one people. Abū Ḥayyān reports this from Ibn ʿAbbās; al-Ālūsī calls that report unusual. Ibn Kathīr argues that Shuʿayb was their kinsman and that the shared command to give full measure and weight confirms a single community; he rejects the two-nation explanation, questions the prophetic attribution of the contrary report, and calls ʿIkrimah's two-mission report weak. Qatādah, as reported by Ibn Kathīr, calls Shuʿayb's people both the People of the Well and the People of the Thicket, citing 50:12 and 50:14. Iṣlāḥī calls the section an account of Shuʿayb and Midian.

turns_on: Whether the different names designate two nations or one community; the notes appeal to Shuʿayb's kinship, the differing punishment reports, and the shared warning about measures and weights.

question: What particular identity or setting is reported for the people addressed?

positions.position: They were pastoral or rural Thicket people, distinct from Midian's town dwellers.
positions.reasons: Al-Rabīʿ, transmitted by Ibn Abī Ḥātim, says herders moved to a spring-fed grove when the lowlands dried, and Shuʿayb warned them before they denied him. Abū Ḥayyān reports the rural versus town distinction; al-Biqāʿī contrasts pastoral people with Shuʿayb the city dweller. Abū Zayd, reported by al-Thaʿlabī, calls them nomads.

positions.position: They were people of Juthām.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās, as reported by al-Wāḥidī, says Shuʿayb was sent to his own people and another people, the Thicket people of Juthām; al-Wāḥidī mentions 7:85 and 11:84.

positions.position: They inhabited seven towns.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah reports seven towns and says Shuʿayb, being from Midian, was not one of their inhabitants.

positions.position: Shuʿayb's people were also called the People of the Well.
positions.reasons: Qatādah, as reported by Ibn Kathīr, identifies them with both the People of the Well and the Thicket people, mentioning 50:12 and 50:14.

turns_on: The notes give different reports of tribal identity, number of settlements, pastoral setting, and another name; they do not argue directly among these details.

question: What does the name of the people addressed, al-Aykah or Laykah, denote?

positions.position: It denotes a dense grove or thicket of intertwined trees.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī calls aykah the singular of ayk and says Arabs use it for densely interwoven trees, citing al-Nābighah's dove-in-a-grove line. Al-Bayḍāwī describes soft trees near Midian. Al-Ālūsī reports the interwoven-tree sense, and cites al-Bukhārī's gloss of both al-Aykah and Laykah as the thicket. Al-Thaʿlabī treats al-Ayka and al-Layka as dialectal forms.

positions.position: It is a particular intertwined dawmah tree.
positions.reasons: Al-Bayḍāwī offers this as another view of the grove; al-Ālūsī includes the dawmah tree among the reported interwoven trees.

positions.position: Al-Aykah names the whole country.
positions.reasons: Al-Ālūsī reports this alternative, comparing its name to Mecca and Bakka; he says the Thicket people remain distinct from Midian on either the grove or country interpretation.

positions.position: Laykah is the proper name of a settlement, possibly a foreign name.
positions.reasons: Abū ʿUbaydah, as reported by al-Ālūsī, cites an exegesis book naming Laykah as a settlement. Al-Bayḍāwī notes the place-name analysis. Al-Ālūsī says absence of an attested Arabic l-y-k root does not exclude a foreign name, and explains its diptote form by proper-name status, foreign origin, and femininity. Al-Zamakhsharī disputes the place-name interpretation, saying Laykah is otherwise unknown.

turns_on: Whether the designation is a common word for trees, one tree, a region, or an independent proper name.

question: How is the people's name read and analyzed?

positions.position: Laykah is read without hamza, with the shifted vowel or a fatḥa, and may be treated as a proper name.
positions.reasons: Al-Bayḍāwī names Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, and Ibn ʿĀmir and explains the vowel shift and spelling without alif. Al-Ālūsī names the two Haramain readers and Ibn ʿĀmir for fatḥa on lām and diptote treatment here and in Ṣād; he also reports the hamza-deletion spelling. Abū ʿUbaydah cites an exegesis book calling Laykah a settlement. Al-Ālūsī defends the reading as one of the seven and mutawātir, argues a foreign proper name can be diptote despite the unattested Arabic root, and says denial of the mutawātir reading approaches apostasy; he names al-Mubarrad, Ibn Qutaybah, al-Zajjāj, al-Fārisī, and al-Naḥḥās as predecessors of al-Zamakhsharī in rejecting it.

positions.position: Al-Aykah is also read with hamza, as the word for the thicket.
positions.reasons: Al-Thaʿlabī says al-Ayka and al-Layka are dialectal forms both read in the Qurʾān; al-Ālūsī reports that al-Bukhārī gives both and glosses them as the thicket. Al-Ālūsī contrasts the spelling of the hamza form with Laykah's pronunciation-based spelling.

positions.position: Laykah is only a pronunciation-based spelling of al-Aykah; treating it as an independent accusative place name is a mistake.
positions.reasons: Al-Zamakhsharī, as reported by al-Ālūsī, says the codex's lack of alif misled readers into treating Laykah as a place name; these two spellings may simply follow pronunciation, the story is one, and Laykah is unknown. Al-Ālūsī rejects this as unsupported because the sevenfold reading is mutawātir, also citing a report from an exegesis book; he adds the possibility of a foreign proper name.

turns_on: Whether the no-hamza form can be a genuine proper name and diptote reading or is merely phonetic spelling mistakenly reanalyzed as a place name.

question: How is Shuʿayb introduced in this address?

positions.position: He is named as the speaker without the title 'their brother'.
positions.reasons: Al-Ālūsī expressly notes the opening's wording: Shuʿayb spoke to them, with no fraternal title.

question: Why is Shuʿayb not called 'their brother' here?

positions.position: He belonged to Midian, not to the Thicket people, so he was not their kinsman.
positions.reasons: Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī's exegetes, al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī reporting Muqātil, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī, and al-Sāmarrāʾī contrast this verse with the 'brother' wording for Midian at 7:85 or 11:84. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah reports that Shuʿayb came from Midian outside their seven towns. Al-Bayḍāwī calls him an outsider to the grove's people. Al-Biqāʿī explains the distinction as a city dweller addressing pastoral people and says the sending of prophets from towns honors settled communities for their shared wisdom and blessing. Al-Sāmarrāʾī contrasts the other Shuʿarāʾ prophets addressing their own peoples, cites al-Kashshāf's same explanation and a hadith that Midian's brother was sent to both peoples, and says contextual differences guide choice of expression.

positions.position: Although he was their kinsman, the fraternal title is omitted because they were associated with worship of the Thicket tree.
positions.reasons: Ibn Kathīr prefers identifying these people with Midian and says their tree worship explains the omission even though Shuʿayb was related to them.

positions.position: The fraternal title is omitted for brevity, though the peoples are the same.
positions.reasons: Ibn Jarīr's explanation is reported by Ibn al-Jawzī alongside his identification of the Thicket people with Midian.

turns_on: Whether the omission marks lack of kinship with a separate people, association with tree worship despite kinship, or simple brevity.

question: What does Shuʿayb ask with 'ألا تتقون'?

positions.position: He calls them to fear God and guard against disobedience and its punishment, including shirk.
positions.reasons: Yaḥyā b. Sallām glosses the question as being wary of God. Al-Biqāʿī glosses taqwā as fear of God. Al-Ṭabarī specifies fear of punishment for disobeying their Lord; al-Bursawī specifies punishment for associating partners with Him. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the summons forbids shirk because the people were polytheists, citing Hūd 11:84. Muqātil and al-Qurṭubī place this call with Shuʿayb's claim to be a trustworthy messenger and command to obey; Muqātil also notes he sought no payment and entrusted his reward to the Lord of the worlds, while al-Ṭabarī says obedience leads to right guidance.

question: What tone does 'ألا تتقون' give Shuʿayb's appeal?

positions.position: It is a gentle and tactful appeal.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyyah describes the question in these terms and mentions 79:18.

question: Why does Shuʿayb's call repeat the formula used by earlier prophets?

positions.position: The recurring call expresses the prophets' single faith and shared mission.
positions.reasons: Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, Ibn ʿAṭiyyah, al-Ṭabrisī, and al-Biqāʿī say the repeated words show shared piety, obedience, sincere or exclusive worship, and taking no fee for preaching. Al-Wāḥidī cites 26:106-109 and includes delivering the message; al-Ṭabrisī adds avoiding sins and says no fee removes a deterrent to acceptance; al-Biqāʿī adds counsel, integrity, and honesty. Yaḥyā b. Sallām calls it a repeated exhortation. Ibn ʿĀshūr notes that Shuʿayb opens like earlier messengers for a reason explained previously. Iṣlāḥī says the opening repeats material of the preceding prophetic account and has already been explained.

question: How does this episode connect with the surrounding and parallel accounts?

positions.position: It continues the pattern of rejected prophetic warnings and points readers to parallel accounts of Midian.
positions.reasons: Al-Thaʿlabī says the preceding destruction of Lot's people is a sign: most did not believe, while God is mighty and merciful. Iṣlāḥī compares Lot's warning about moral misconduct with Shuʿayb's warning about economic misconduct; the people persisted, shared the other nations' fate, and their account closes with repeated verses. Asad directs readers to his note on 7:85 and the fuller Shuʿayb and Midian narrative at 11:84-95. Ibn ʿĀshūr invokes 11:84 for the people's polytheism.
